Listen to this article Share A coalition of five European Union (EU) member states, Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark, and the Netherlands are set to announce an agreement to transfer rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, marking an aggressive escalation in Europe’s bid to curb irregular migration. Expected to be unveiled in Vienna on today, Monday, November 16, 2026, the arrangement follows the EU’s adoption of its new Returns Regulation, which permits member states to establish external return facilities outside the bloc. Unlike the United Kingdom’s (UK) scrapped asylum scheme which sought to offshore applicants while their claims were still under review, the European model will target migrants who have exhausted all legal appeals to remain in the EU. As European governments face mounting domestic pressure ahead of key elections, officials argue that outsourcing deportations will deter prospective migrants from paying smugglers for difficult journeys across the Mediterranean. However, human rights advocates have raised sharp legal and ethical alarms over transferring individuals to a third country with which they have no prior ties. “What recourse do people have if their rights are violated and who is accountable?” asked Céline Mias, EU director at the Danish Refugee Council, questioning how state responsibility would function in practice. Read also: Reforms must outlive political tenures to deliver lasting impact – Aig-Imoukhuede Foundation Migration researchers have similarly cast doubt on whether offshore return hubs actually reduce irregular arrivals over the long term. “Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or change route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices,” observed Roberto Forin, a migration specialist at the Mixed Migration Centre. Echoing those concerns, the Council of Europe previously warned that external return hubs carry significant human rights risks. Despite longstanding international criticism over its domestic political freedoms, surveillance, and alleged backing of the M23 rebel group in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda has steadily positioned itself as a willing migration partner for Western governments. Kigali previously entered a transfer agreement with the United States (US) in 2025 to accept up to 250 deportees, and demanded £50 million ($63.6 million) from London after the UK Supreme Court ruled Britain’s original scheme unlawful in 2023. The deal signals a hardening European border regime that increasingly externalizes migration control onto African soil. While European policymakers view the measure as a deterrent against irregular journeys through the Sahara and Mediterranean, it also underscores the growing urgency for Nigerian authorities to expand legal labour mobility pathways, strengthen domestic job creation, and address the economic push factors driving high-risk youth migration.
